name: Agneeswarar Temple, Melai Tirukkattupalli
deity: Shiva as Agneeswarar (Theeyadiappar), with the goddess Soundaryanayaki (Azhagammai)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Kaveri delta, sung in the Tevaram by Sambandar and Appar (7th century); the present structure is later and not firmly dated
dynasty: Medieval patrons of the Chola country (specific dynasty not firmly sourced)
summary: Agneeswarar Temple at Melai Tirukkattupalli, on the southern bank of the Kudamurutti, is a Tevaram shrine where Agni, the god of fire, is remembered as having been cleansed of the sins he carried, and whose sanctum lies below the level of the courtyard.

sections.history: Melai Tirukkattupalli lies on the southern bank of the Kudamurutti river in Thanjavur district, some fifteen to eighteen kilometres west of Thiruvaiyaru. The word melai, meaning western or upstream, distinguishes it from Keezhai Tirukkattuppalli, the sister shrine of the same name nearer the sea. Both Sambandar and Appar sang of Shiva in this place, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam of the Chola country on the south bank of the Kaveri. Since the saints knew the shrine in the seventh century, its worship is clearly older than the stone that stands today. The present structure is later and cannot be firmly dated, and the temple has been reported to be under renovation in recent years, but through all of it the daily worship goes on.
sections.architecture: The temple is entered beneath a five-tiered gopuram and is enclosed by three concentric corridors, which give it the layered calm of a traditional Chola-country shrine. Its most unusual feature lies within. The sanctum of Agneeswarar sits at a subterranean level, so that the worshipper descends to the Lord, and the Shiva linga is a self-manifested one, modest in size and crowned with a five-hooded serpent. The goddess Soundaryanayaki, also called Azhagammai, is honoured as the Lord's consort. The sacred Agni Teertham, once a tank and today remembered in the form of a well, is associated with the god of fire's own worship.
sections.legends: The temple takes its name from Agni, the god of fire. As the carrier of every offering burnt in the sacrificial fires, Agni felt the weight of all those sins upon himself, and everything he touched was scorched and blackened. He turned to Shiva for release, and was told to bathe in the water of this place and worship there. Having done so he was cleansed, and the Lord who received his worship came to be called Agneeswarar, while the village was remembered as Agneeswaram. A second tradition, told in several versions, speaks of a king of Uraiyur and sevvanthi flowers meant only for Shiva, given instead to the royal ladies; when the offering was misused, sand is said to have rained on Uraiyur until the king and queen came here in repentance. The tellings differ in their details, but they agree on the compassion shown to those who return in sincerity.
sections.festivals: The year's great celebration is the Panguni Peruvizha, the annual festival of the month of Panguni in March or April. Masi Magam in February or March, Maha Shivaratri, the Aipasi Annabishekam in October or November, when the Lord is adorned with offerings of rice, and Margazhi Tiruvadhirai in December or January are all kept with devotion, and the monthly Pradosham is observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Come to Melai Tirukkattupalli for a quiet, unhurried darshan. Step down into the sanctum of Agneeswarar, one of the few Shiva temples where the descent itself becomes part of the prayer, and then turn to the goddess Soundaryanayaki. The corridors and the well of Agni Teertham reward a slow walk, and devotees who seek relief from a burden they carry, whether of conscience or of worry, find the story of Agni a gentle companion here. The village sits by the Kudamurutti among green fields, and the temple is best combined with the other Tevaram shrines of this part of the delta.

visit.timings: Typically open from about 6:00 to 11:00 in the morning and from about 4:00 to 8:30 in the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days and while renovation work continues.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tirukkattupalli (PIN 613104) lies about 24 km from Thanjavur and roughly 15 to 18 km west of Thiruvaiyaru, on the southern bank of the Kudamurutti. Buses from Thanjavur and Tiruchirappalli serve the town. The nearest railway station is Budhalur, about 8 km away, with Thanjavur Junction the main railhead. Tiruchirappalli, around 45 to 50 km to the west, has the nearest airport.
